reason: The text presents Samson's narrative, which demonstrates leadership characteristics antithetical to the stated model. While Samson was divinely appointed to 'begin to save Israel from the hand of the Philistines,' his actual conduct shows: (1) actions driven by personal desires and grievances rather than communal welfare (pursuing a Philistine wife despite parental objection); (2) lack of accountability to his people—he hides his actions from parents and community, acts unilaterally without consulting leadership; (3) impulsive violence motivated by personal vengeance rather than systematic responsibility for his people's liberation; (4) no demonstration of organized leadership or coordination with his community for collective defense. When confronted by Judahite men regarding consequences, he blames them rather than taking responsibility. His final act is personal suicide/revenge. While his strength serves divine purposes, the narrative portrays him as an individual with extraordinary power pursuing personal ends, not as a model of responsible, accountable leadership concerned with his people's systematic welfare and collective well-being.
